documentation.range: The Longsnout Pipefish is extant in the Northeast and Eastern Central Atlantic from the Baltic Sea and near the Faroe Islands, Norway down through the North Sea and British Isles to Guinea-Bissau, including the Azores and Canary Islands (Dawson 1986, GBIF 2024). It is found throughout the Mediterranean and Black seas (Dawson 1986, GBIF 2024) and has been identified in Lake Bafa, Türkiye (Gürkan and Innal 2018).
documentation.population: There are no population size estimates for this pipefish. The trend is suspected to be stable or increasing due to its ability to use multiple habitat types and recent stability or recovery of seagrass habitats across its range.
documentation.habitats:
The Longsnout Pipefish is a demersal species that inhabits coastal and estuarine areas with macroalgae and seagrass beds, such as Zostera species (Hernández-Urcera et al. 2021), but  can also be found in rocky, sandy, and gravel substrates and rhodolith beds (Planas et al. 2021). It uses seagrasses as breeding and feeding grounds and as shelter from predators. This pipefish occurs at depths of 3–110 m (Dawson 1986, Lazic unpubl. data 2024). It mostly feeds on small crustaceans such as amphipods, isopods and carideans (Gürkan and Taskavak 2019, Gürkan et al. 2021, Planas et al. 2021) but also on barnacle cypris larvae and other prey. Gürkan et al. (2009) speculate that the large variation in average sizes at maturity is due to water temperatures. Subpopulations inhabiting colder seas tend to reach sexual maturity later, and thus reach a longer length in comparison to species found in warmer temperatures.

Males give birth to fully formed juveniles (up to ca. 200) measuring an average of 2.6 cm. Adult range in length is highly variable depending on the region. The length range is 3.1–25.6 cm in Turkish populations (Gürkan et al. 2009), and 14.1–49.8 cm in NE Spain (Planas et al. 2021, Planas 2022).

In a study by Silva et al. (2006) on the early life history behaviour of this pipefish, it was observed that newborn juveniles immediately adopted a benthic strategy, and kept close, continual contact with the strata. This behaviour was thought to limit the species' ability to disperse and colonize new areas in comparison to species with a pelagic early life stage. It may result in an increased vulnerability to habitat fragmentation and degradation. Furthermore, it can migrate to more sheltered sites before the seaweed assemblages vanish in autumn and winter due to storms and strong sea currents (Planas et al. 2021).
documentation.threats:
This species is threatened by seagrass and kelp degradation due to climate change. Although kelps have declined slightly in recent decades (Wernberg et al. 2019), seagrasses have stabilized or are increasing slightly since 2000 (Dunic et al. 2021).

Species distribution modelling for European syngnathids by Monteiro et al. (2023), found that under various climate scenarios, the change in suitable habitat for the Longsnout Pipefish ranges from 88.0 to 93.0% retained by 2040–2050 and 83.1–91.0% retained by 2090–2100. Populations in semi-enclosed areas such as the Baltic Sea, Black Sea, and Mediterranean are expected to experience the most drastic changes (Monteiro et al. 2023).
documentation.measures: Currently there are no known conservation actions in place for this species and it does not appear in any international legislation, but its distribution overlaps with multiple Marine Protected Areas, including the Atlantic Islands of Galicia National Park (Planas et al. 2021). Population and habitat monitoring are needed.
documentation.use_trade: Some pipefish species are caught as bycatch and subsequently used as a substitute for seahorses (Hippocampus spp.) in traditional Chinese medicine (Vincent et al. 2011). However, it is claimed that the Longsnout Pipefish is mistakenly identified in records of Chinese medicine (Jiang et al. 2019). It is not clear whether the Longsnout Pipefish is of interest for the aquarium trade.
documentation.rationale: The Longsnout Pipefish (Syngnathus acus) is a long (to 50 cm total length) syngnathiform fish that occurs in the Northeast and Eastern Central Atlantic, as well as the Mediterranean and the Black Seas at depths of 3–110 m. This pipefish inhabits macroalgal and seagrass beds, and over rock, sand and gravel substrates. Although it may suffer from localized seagrass habitat degradation and loss due to coastal development, pollution, and climate change, it can use other habitat types and is projected to maintain >85% of its habitat through 2100 based on species distribution models. Its population size is suspected to be stable, and thus does not approach thresholds for a threatened assessment under criterion A. It has a wide range and is not likely to meet thresholds for a small population. Therefore, the Longsnout Pipefish is assessed as Least Concern.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Previously, Syngnathus temminckii was included as a synonym of S. acus. However, S. temminckii is a valid species, and the southern African portion of the previously assessed S. acus is in fact under that name (Mwale et al. 2013).
